doc.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The Dick Cavett Show and staff pay
summary: He plays Cavett and Merv Griffin; staff pay was salaried and strings were kept on sustaining salary.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Then you were on The Dick Cavett Show, weren’t you, for a long time?
I did The Dick Cavett Show from the time it started until it went off the air. And I used to do – at ABC, on radio, we also did The Merv Griffin Show, when he had his show on radio. We did that.
Was it different to play for radio and play for television? Would you be on camera sometimes for television?
Oh yeah. When we were doing a television show, sometimes we were.
Would you be paid according to whether you were on camera?
It was just a straight salary?
There was a staff scale, a regular scale for the networks, and that’s what you were paid on a weekly basis. But you got that every week.
Regardless of playing one show or five shows.

That’s right. That’s true. You got your full salary. Sometimes, if, for instance – we had a tremendous string section on staff. Sometimes they would know in advance that for the next six months, they’re not going to have a show in which they use strings. Then they would put them on what they call “sustaining salary,” which was less than the regular scale that they got.
But they could go off and do what they needed to do.
Oh sure. They could do whatever they wanted to do, and they were still collecting the salary there.
That sounds like, for a musician who lived an itinerant life, which most musicians do, this was a very good . . . .
It was excellent. It was very good.
What was playing on the Cavett Show like?

That was nice. We used to play – they didn’t feature the band very often, but whenever we’d go in and out of a commercial, we would be playing something. We had a chance to play – in the studio, we did a lot of playing. We entertained the audience. Dick always had very interesting guests.
